content.title: About
content.content: Bagel with raisins is a traditional ring‑shaped bread product with a dense crust and a soft interior, featuring sweet raisins folded into the dough. It combines the subtle sweetness of raisins with the characteristic aroma of caraway seeds often used in bagel recipes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bagels originated in Eastern European Jewish cuisine and became popular in the United States in the early 20th century.
The classic preparation method involves boiling short dough rings in water with baking soda before baking, giving the bagel its distinctive chewy crust.
Raisins are usually pre‑soaked in hot water to become plump and aromatic before being incorporated into the dough.
Bagels are commonly served with cream cheese, smoked salmon, or simply butter.
In Russia, bagels with raisins are often found in bakeries during the New Year holiday season.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Both the raisins and the whole‑grain flour used in the bagel provide dietary fiber that supports digestive health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Raisins are rich in polyphenols, which help combat oxidative stress in the body.

items.title: Enriched with B‑vitamins
items.content: Bagel dough typically contains thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates from the dough and natural sugars from raisins offers a fast source of energy, making it a good pre‑exercise snack.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It provides iron, potassium, and magnesium, essential for normal bodily functions.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Raisins increase the overall sugar level of the product, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Bagel with raisins is relatively calorie‑dense; excessive consumption may contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional bagels are made with wheat flour, making them unsuitable for individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sulfur dioxide
items.content: Some raisins are treated with sulfur dioxide, which can cause reactions in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bagel with raisins can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, sliced and spread with cream cheese, hummus, or nut butter. It also works well in sandwiches, paired with ham, vegetables, or avocado.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bagel in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, keep it in the refrigerator (up to 5 days) or freeze, wrapped in plastic, for up to 3 months. Warm in a toaster or oven before eating.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-meat-an.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with meat and dark‑green vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of eggs prepared as an omelet or scrambled, combined with lean meat (such as chicken breast or turkey) and dark‑green vegetables (spinach, broccoli, kale). Eggs provide high‑quality protein, while the vegetables are rich in vitamins, minerals and antioxidants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs contain all essential amino acids needed by the human body.
Dark‑green vegetables like spinach provide over 20% of the daily value of vitamin K.
Poultry meat is one of the leanest sources of animal protein, low in saturated fat.
Cooking eggs as an omelet retains more nutrients compared with prolonged frying.
The combination of protein and vegetables enhances iron absorption from the meat.

items.title: Complete high‑quality protein
items.content: Eggs and meat supply all essential amino acids, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and meat provide vitamin B12, while dark‑green vegetables are a good source of folate (B9), important for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Spinach and broccoli contain lutein, zeaxanthin and vitamin C, which help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Bone support
items.content: Vitamin K and calcium from the greens contribute to bone mineralization.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Choosing lean meat and using minimal oil makes the dish suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg white proteins.

items.title: Improperly cooked meat
items.content: Undercooked poultry can harbor harmful bacteria; ensure thorough cooking.

items.title: Oxalates in greens
items.content: Large amounts of spinach can increase oxalate intake, which may be problematic for people prone to kidney stones.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: While eggs are nutritious, people with high cholesterol should monitor portion size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beat the eggs, add diced lean meat and pre‑cooked or lightly sautéed dark‑green vegetables. Cook in a non‑stick pan with a small amount of olive oil, stirring until the desired consistency is reached. Season with pepper, paprika, or fresh herbs as desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The dish is best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a pan or microwave, adding a little oil to prevent drying out.

light-ice-cream-cone-chocolate-prepackag.title: Light Ice Cream Cone, Chocolate, Prepackaged

content.title: About
content.content: Light ice cream cone is a ready‑to‑eat dessert consisting of a crisp waffle cone filled with a thin layer of chocolate ice cream. The product is packaged in individual portions, providing convenience for storage and transport.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The waffle cone is made from whole‑grain flour, making it lighter than traditional sweet cones.
The chocolate ice cream contains natural cocoa butter, giving it a characteristic aroma and creamy texture.
The packaging is made from biodegradable material suitable for composting.
Each portion is designed for a single serving – about 80 g of product.
The product contains no artificial colors or flavors.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Light ice cream contains less fat than traditional creamy versions, making it more suitable for diet‑conscious eating.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The dairy base of the ice cream provides a significant amount of calcium essential for bone health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa butter is rich in polyphenols, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Carbohydrates from the milk and waffle cone quickly supply the body with energy.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Thanks to its fine crystalline structure, the ice cream melts quickly in the mouth and is easy to digest.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: The product contains milk, which may trigger reactions in individuals allergic to lactose or casein.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Despite the light formula, added sugar is present, which should be considered by people with diabetes.

items.title: Temperature sensitivity
items.content: Storing above +4 °C can cause the ice cream to melt, altering its texture and flavor.

items.title: Choking hazard for children
items.content: Small chocolate particles may pose a choking risk for children under 3 years old.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready to eat straight from the package. Optionally, garnish with berries, nuts, or a dusting of cocoa powder. Hold the cone by the base to avoid breakage.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a freezer at –18 °C or lower. After opening, consume within 24 hours. Do not keep at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato hash brown is a dish made from grated potatoes that are pan‑fried or deep‑fried until crisp and golden. It is commonly served as a side or snack in restaurants, offering a crunchy exterior and a soft interior, usually seasoned with salt and spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recorded recipes for shredded potato dishes date back to the 19th century in the United States.
Hash browns are a staple breakfast item in American diners and fast‑food chains.
There are many variations: with cheese, bacon, onions, or herbs.
In some countries they are shaped into round patties, in others they are served as flat cakes.
Hash browns can be cooked in oil or baked in the oven for a lighter version.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Potatoes provide complex carbs that supply lasting energy and help keep you feeling full.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Hash browns contain vitamin B6 and folate, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potatoes are a good source of potassium, important for blood pressure regulation and muscle function.

items.title: Low sodium (when lightly salted)
items.content: If prepared with minimal added salt, hash browns can fit into a balanced diet.

items.title: Fiber
items.content: Grated potatoes retain some dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: High calorie content when fried
items.content: Cooking in oil adds significant calories and fat, so portion size should be monitored.

items.title: Rare potato allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to potatoes.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: Over‑cooking at high temperatures can produce acrylamide, a potentially harmful compound; aim for a golden‑brown color, not dark brown.

items.title: Salt
items.content: Excessive salt can contribute to hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hash browns are served hot as a side to meat, fish or vegetables, used in burgers, or enjoyed as a snack with dips such as ketchup, mayo, or ranch dressing. They can also be crumbled over salads for added crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked hash browns in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. Frozen hash browns keep up to 3 months; they can be cooked directly from frozen without fully thawing.

content.title: About
content.content: Scalloped potatoes are thinly sliced potatoes baked in a creamy cheese sauce. They are a common side dish in fast‑food restaurants and diners, served hot as a garnish or a main item.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the United States in the early 19th century and quickly entered fast‑food menus.
Traditional recipes use cream, milk, cheddar cheese, and often onions.
Variations may include bacon, mushrooms, or herbs such as rosemary.
Scalloped potatoes are frequently served in individual ramekins for portion control.

items.title: Potassium source
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which supports heart and muscle function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B6 and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Provide sustained energy release.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese adds calcium, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The creamy sauce and cheese make the dish calorie‑dense; portion size should be monitored.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cream and cheese contain saturated fats, which can affect cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Lactose
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Cheese is often salty, raising the sodium content of the dish.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Scalloped potatoes are served hot, either as a standalone portion or as a side to meat dishes. Eat with a fork, optionally topping with extra cheese or fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in the oven to retain a crispy top.

content.title: About
content.content: A turkey sandwich with cheese is a sandwich or sub made with thinly sliced turkey breast, melted cheese, fresh vegetables and sauce, served on a soft roll. It is commonly offered in fast‑food restaurants and cafés.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey is a lean source of protein popular in the US and Europe.
Sub‑style sandwiches got their name from “submarine” because the roll resembles a submarine hull.
Cheese is often chosen to melt well, such as processed cheese, cheddar or mozzarella.
Some restaurants add cranberry sauce to turkey for a sweet‑savory contrast.
Turkey sandwiches are frequently served with fries or a side salad.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Turkey provides complete protein that supports muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Turkey breast contains less saturated fat than many other meats.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese adds calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey and cheese supply B6 and B12 vitamins, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Fiber from vegetables
items.content: Added lettuce, tomato, cucumber, etc., increase dietary fiber, aiding digestion.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Processed meats and sauces often contain high salt levels; those with hypertension should watch portions.

items.title: Proper cooking of turkey
items.content: Undercooked turkey may harbor harmful bacteria; cook to an internal temperature of 165 °F (74 °C).

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: A cheese‑laden sandwich can be calorie‑rich; portion control is advisable for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is typically eaten by hand, often cut in half. It pairs well with fries, a side salad, or a beverage. For a lighter option, choose a whole‑grain roll and reduced‑fat cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed fresh. If you need to store it, wrap tightly in plastic film and keep refrigerated for up to 24 hours. Store turkey and cheese separately in airtight containers.
